newsitem.title: USA: Clinton turns to ticklish decision on line-item veto.
newsitem.headline: Clinton turns to ticklish decision on line-item veto.

text.p: Having signed into law the balanced-budget agreement painstakingly negotiated with the Republican-led Congress, President Bill Clinton must decide whether to punch a few holes in it by using the line-item veto.

Analysts are divided over whether Clinton will choose the balanced-budget legislation as his first target for the veto, which allows a president to block parts of spending bills or to strike down narrowly targeted tax breaks.

Some argue that Clinton, a Democrat, may not wish to violate the spirit of bipartisanship that helped produce the budget pact, which aims to eliminate the U.S. budget deficit by the year 2002 while offering $95 billion in tax breaks.
"The spirit in which it was put together would push in the direction of no line-item veto," said budget analyst Robert Reischauer of the Brookings Institution think tank.

But Reischauer said the question was a finely balanced one, putting the chances of no veto at only 55 percent, and other analysts said Clinton will not hesitate to use the veto merely because of bipartisanship.
"This era of good feeling is phony and short-lived ... I don't see that as being a big impediment (to using the veto)," said Burson Marstellar budget expert Stan Collender.
"If he line-item vetoes something that is over the top as far as pork barrel (spending) or special interests (on taxes), that is going to be difficult for the Republicans to defend."
Under the law Clinton has five working days -- until next Monday -- to use the veto. Congress could then override any line-item veto by a two-thirds majority vote in both houses.

The law, passed last year, was touted as a way of reducing the deficit by stripping out special-interest items in the budget. Most analysts, however, see its deficit-cutting impact as limited and say its significance lies in the added leverage it gives the president in his negotiations with Congress.

Robert Greenstein, an analyst with the Centre on Budget and Policy Priorities, argued that using the line-item veto now could help Clinton in his dealings with Congress on the spending bills that will come his way in September.

"Showing that he does not shrink from exercising the line- item veto where merited ... may strengthen his hand a bit in bargaining and negotiations on the appropriations bills and other legislation," Greenstein said.
The White House is reviewing the $95 billion tax-cut bill that Clinton signed into law on Tuesday, concentrating on the 79 provisions identified as benefiting narrow constituencies.

Speaking on Monday, Clinton said he was ready to use the veto, but did not tip his hand. "If we have it, it ought to be used. I believe that it ought to be used somewhat sparingly," he said. "My experience as governor was that once I used it a few times ... I didn't need to use it very much anymore."

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton would have a recommendation by the end of the week. "They're looking at each of the provisions ... to (decide) whether they are good economic policy, good social policy, good tax policy."
Several analysts argued that the decision turns more on the politics of the question than on the substance.
"In my view, the merits will matter much less than the political and the legal considerations," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.

This analyst argued Clinton may use the veto where he will have the best chance of fighting off the legal challenge he is likely to face to the law, arguing that this may militate for holding off until the spending bills in September.
How much political opposition Clinton will face to the use of a line-item veto is open to question, with many Democrats and even some Republicans saying they would support him.
"If there are provisions ... that are clearly outrageous, I would support the president doing it," John Kasich, the Ohio Republican who chairs the House Budget Committee, said Sunday.
